guides.title: Where should I start?
guides.text: Start here gives an overview, the headline numbers and the Promise Clock. Then open Argument Bank: choose a current case or describe a new one, and inspect similar TrialWatch cases and report excerpts. Use Stress Test for the Indonesian reform example, UN Letter to prepare a sourced draft, and Outcome Updates to see verified changes after a report. A lawyer should review any legal use.

guides.title: How does Argument Bank work?
guides.text: Open Argument Bank. Choose a case or describe a new case using charge, speech, role and region filters. Explore By argument or By case, and open the report page links to check the original text. Similarity is not a prediction, and a good outcome following advocacy does not prove advocacy caused it.

guides.title: What does Stress Test mean?
guides.text: Stress Test applies this project's draft Indonesian reform rules to recorded facts. LIKELY BARRED means R1 or R2 fired; AT RISK means R3 or R4 fired without R1 or R2; STILL PROSECUTABLE means none of those rules fired. These labels describe the rule check, not the defendant's personal risk or a court outcome. Review the reasons and the sensitivity analysis; missing facts limit the result.

guides.title: How do I prepare a UN letter?
guides.text: Open UN Letter, choose or describe a case, inspect the numbered sources, then use Draft with Gemini or Build plain draft (no AI). Review and edit the draft, check citations and source support, and complete the reviewer checks before saving. The website does not submit the letter to the UN.

guides.title: What is the Promise Clock?
guides.text: The Promise Clock on Start here counts the days since each official pledge about Indonesia's reformed ITE Law and shows the evidence that it has been carried out. Open Evidence on a card to read the sources. Partly kept means there is evidence the pledge is applied, but also gaps or counter-examples.

guides.title: Can I trust the answers?
guides.text: This is an independent hackathon project. Answers are guidance for review, not legal advice. Answers about legal standards come from a curated library of TrialWatch report excerpts and show the exact passages they rely on, with a link to the report page. Open the original report to check. The guide does not search the web or read case forms.

guides.title: What happens to my questions?
guides.text: Your questions are answered inside the app from the curated guide and library text; they are not sent to an outside service, and case data and forms are not read. Even so, don't paste confidential or sensitive case details. Clear chat removes the conversation from this session.

answers.question: What is the three-part test for restricting speech?
answers.answer: Under Article 19 of the ICCPR, a restriction on speech is lawful only if it passes three tests: it must be provided by law, serve a legitimate objective, and be necessary and proportionate to that objective [reading-indonesia]. The UN Human Rights Committee says such limits must be strictly and narrowly tailored [reading-proportionality]. TrialWatch reports apply this test to each prosecution, for example the reports on Indonesia vs. Suzethe Margaret and Turkey v. Veysel Ok.

evidence.quote: restrictions on the right to freedom of expression must (i) be provided by law (the principle of legality), (ii) serve a legitimate objective, and (iii) be necessary to achieve and proportionate to that objective
any limitations on the Article 19 right to freedom of expression must be strictly and narrowly tailored in accordance with a three-part test

answers.question: Why do vague laws violate the principle of legality?
answers.answer: The legality prong requires a law to be precise enough for people to regulate their conduct, and it must not give unfettered discretion to those who enforce it [reading-legality]. The TrialWatch report on Poland's Article 196 found that a subjective offence, offending religious feelings, gave the authorities broad discretion and was ripe for abuse; such a law fails the test even if the other two prongs are met [reading-vagueness].

evidence.quote: formulated with sufficient precision to enable an individual to regulate his or her conduct accordingly
Article 196’s imprecision gives the authorities broad discretion in making charging decisions, rendering it ripe for abuse
even if the government could demonstrate the law complied with the latter two requirements, it would contravene the threshold legality requirement

answers.question: What makes a law overbroad?
answers.answer: A law is overbroad when it reaches far more speech than needed and leaves the authorities unbounded discretion. The TrialWatch report on Malaysia v. Malaysiakini and Steven Gan notes that laws cannot be overbroad, and cites the UN Special Rapporteur: restrictions must be precise, public and transparent, and must not give the authorities unbounded discretion [reading-broadness].

evidence.quote: the restriction must be provided by laws that are precise, public and transparent; it must avoid providing authorities with unbounded discretion

answers.question: Can prison be a proportionate penalty for speech?
answers.answer: TrialWatch reports treat prison for speech as very hard to justify. The report on Kazakhstan v. Nazym Tabyldieva found that the possibility of imprisonment clearly failed the third prong of the three-part test [reading-necessity]. Even a restriction with a legitimate aim fails the necessity test if the protection could be achieved in less restrictive ways [reading-necessity].

evidence.quote: provides for potential imprisonment clearly fails the third prong of the Human Rights Committee’s three-part test
violate[] the test of necessity if the protection could be achieved in other ways that do not restrict freedom of

answers.question: When is detention arbitrary?
answers.answer: Detention can be arbitrary even when domestic law allows it. The UN Human Rights Committee reads arbitrariness broadly, to include inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process, and the tests of reasonableness, necessity and proportionality [reading-detention]. The TrialWatch report on 15 post-election trials in Belarus adds that the Committee generally considers mass arrests during demonstrations to be arbitrary [reading-detention].

evidence.quote: arrest or detention may be authorized by domestic law and nonetheless be arbitrary
elements of inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process of law
the Human Rights Committee generally considers mass arrests, including during demonstrations, to be arbitrary

answers.question: What does the presumption of innocence require?
answers.answer: The presumption of innocence is a cornerstone of a fair trial: anyone accused of a crime must be treated as innocent until proven guilty under a procedure set by domestic and international law. The TrialWatch report on Belarus v. Katsiaryna Andreyeva and Daria Chultsova sets out this standard [reading-fair-trial].

evidence.quote: The presumption of innocence is a cornerstone of the right to a fair trial
anyone accused of a crime be considered innocent until proven guilty

answers.question: How do these standards apply in Indonesia?
answers.answer: TrialWatch has applied the same test in Indonesia. The report on Indonesia vs. Suzethe Margaret, by Dr Charles O’Mahony, notes that the UN Human Rights Committee places a high value on uninhibited expression and requires restrictions to be provided by law, serve a legitimate objective, and be necessary and proportionate [reading-indonesia]. To see how Indonesia's 2024–25 ITE reform affects past cases, open Stress Test [help-stress].
